views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Continue the high-level negotiations toward a settlement — do not escalate, and do not rush to over-concede. This is the winning moment to convert the US's own postponed tariff hikes (twice delayed from the 25% level) and its eagerness for a deal into maximum relief, while withholding final concession on enforcement/sequencing until we are guaranteed the removal of the tariffs covering roughly $250B of our exports. Hold the line on structural IP/enforcement terms so a deal genuinely relieves pressure rather than merely locking in US demands.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is real and substantial but not existential, which is why I score it at +0.35 rather than higher. US Section 301 tariffs blanket roughly $250B of our exports (10% on List 3, 25% on $50B), and firm-level targeting is active — ZTE was denied US components and DOJ unsealed Huawei/Meng charges and sought extradition (event timeline 2018-09-24, 2019-01-28). The economic drag is visible: China's manufacturing export-orders index fell to a decade low in February 2019 as the frontloading effect wore off (The Diplomat, 2019-03-05), though March Caixin PMI rebounded above 50 on stimulus (CNN, 2019-04-01) — so the economy is soft but not collapsing. That keeps the threat moderate. However, the trajectory is genuinely de-escalatory and we hold meaningful leverage: the scheduled 25% hike has been postponed twice (2019-02-24, 2019-03-01), our retaliation on US soy/farm imports is putting political pressure on the US farm belt (Grassley on Iowa farm impact; Reuters 2019-03-29), and both presidents want a deal, with a Mar-a-Lago summit targeted for late April (CNN 2019-03-19; CNBC 2019-04-02). Given that the US itself has moved toward us and our leverage is real, this is not a moment for escalation — further retaliation would kill the talks and trigger the very 25% hike we want to avoid — nor for a capitulation. The stickiest issue is the US demand for an enforcement mechanism with re-imposition of tariffs and its reluctance to lift tariffs immediately (CNBC 2019-03-28, 2019-04-02); we should trade final concessions on enforcement only for concrete tariff removal, keeping a firm negotiating posture without new commitments.
key_factors: ~$250B of US tariffs on Chinese exports at 10-25%, with the 25% List-3 hike postponed twice as talks progressed (2019-02-24, 2019-03-01)
Firm-level targeting active: ZTE denial order (2018-04-16) and DOJ Huawei/Meng charges + extradition request (2019-01-28)
China retaliatory tariffs on US soy/autos/aircraft (~$60B+) pressuring the US farm belt and domestic politics
Negotiations in crunch period: Liu He in Washington 2019-04-03, progress on text/enforcement, Mar-a-Lago summit eyed late April; enforcement + tariff-lift sequencing the remaining hurdles
Chinese economy soft but cushioned: Feb 2019 export-order PMI decade low, but March Caixin PMI rebound above 50 on stimulus

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. Combined Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
US DOJ unseals charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests extradition.
Trump delays scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%.
Intensive Washington talks; both sides report progress on text including enforcement. No deal signed.
Chances increasing for a deal; negotiations 'critical' over enforcement mechanism and plan to lift US tariffs.
China makes unprecedented proposals on tech transfer; IP and enforcement remain sticking points.
China March PMI: factories defying slowdown; stimulus starting to bear fruit; tariffs on ~$250B of exports.
China export-orders PMI fell to a decade low in February 2019 as frontloading effect wears off; stimulus intensifies.
